slides.title: Appendix B: Review of Tensors
slides.notes: Open the appendix as a working grammar for later Riemannian geometry, not as a vocabulary list. The lecture goal is to recognize tensorial objects by their slots, their chart behavior, and the operations that survive a change of coordinates. Keep pointing students back to what can be checked locally.

slides.title: The Appendix as a Dependency Map
slides.notes: Use the artifact as a reading map. The central node is not meant to be decorative; it tells us that tensors, bundles, forms, and integration are mutually reinforcing. Ask which edge would break if a student treated tensors as arrays without tracking the vector spaces on which they act.

slides.title: Tensors Are Multilinear Slot Machines
slides.notes: Emphasize that the type of a tensor is bookkeeping with consequences. Covariant slots eat vectors, contravariant slots eat covectors, and multilinearity is the rule that makes local computations meaningful. The slide deliberately separates slots before mentioning coordinates, because coordinates should serve the object rather than define it.

slides.title: Coordinate Change Is the Stress Test
slides.notes: This is the first operational test. Components can change, but the tensor must encode the same multilinear measurement after the basis changes. Present the blue and teal factors as paired compensation: one part changes the vector inputs, the other part changes the recorded components.

slides.title: From One Vector Space to a Tensor Bundle
slides.notes: Move from linear algebra at one point to fields over a manifold. A tensor bundle is a smooth assignment of the appropriate tensor space over every point. The critical phrase is smooth assignment; without that, we only have unrelated algebraic fibers and no geometric object to differentiate or integrate.

slides.title: Differential Forms Add Antisymmetry
slides.notes: Forms are tensors with a built-in orientation detector. The wedge product is not just notation for multiplication; it records signed area, volume, and higher dimensional oriented measurement. This prepares students for Stokes type statements later because boundaries and signs must be encoded before integration begins.

slides.title: Densities Integrate Without Choosing Orientation
slides.notes: Contrast forms and densities carefully. A top form is naturally integrated once an orientation is chosen, while a density transforms with absolute Jacobian weight and therefore avoids sign changes under orientation reversal. This distinction matters whenever the manifold is not oriented or when volume should remain positive.

slides.title: Local Chart Metric Check
slides.notes: The local chart artifact gives a concrete sanity check. The determinant expression is positive, so the displayed coordinate model behaves like a valid local metric model in the sampled region. The curvature proxy is not a theorem here; it is a computational inspection surface for seeing how coordinate data can carry geometric information.

slides.title: Invariant Checks: What Survives the Model
slides.notes: Read the JSON checks as a miniature test suite for the appendix. Connectedness checks the concept graph, entropy prevents the vocabulary from collapsing into one label, and the Vandermonde collision test models a degeneracy. These are not textbook theorems, but they train the same habit: identify what should remain stable.

slides.title: What This Appendix Supplies Later
slides.notes: End by tying the review to later chapters. Curvature, Ricci contraction, metric compatibility, forms, and densities all require the tensor grammar from this appendix. The recap should leave students with a diagnostic question: when a formula appears later, which slots does it have and what change of coordinates does it survive?
